title: Between Two Rivers: Nakajima and Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park
standfirst: Where the Ota River forks into the Motoyasu and Hon channels stood Nakajima, a wedge of reclaimed land that grew from reed banks into one of Hiroshima's busiest commercial quarters. The atomic bomb of 6 August 1945 erased it within seconds. On the same ground, planners and the architect Kenzo Tange built Peace Memorial Park. This dossier traces both layers.

sections.heading: A delta built from a river's silt

paragraphs.text: Hiroshima sits on the delta the Ota River built at the head of the Inland Sea. A 1925 city guide reproduces a geologist's estimate that it took the river's silt roughly one thousand and seventy years to raise the mudflats into land, a slow accumulation that first became habitable as reed-covered sandbars and then, hamlet by hamlet, as farmland. Old villages on the delta were known together as Goka-no-sho, the 'five hamlets,' each said to sit on its own patch of ground like an island in the reeds. Where the river's main branch forked near the tip of one such patch, a 1900 Hiroshima guidebook records, the stream split into an eastern channel called the Motoyasu and a western one called the Hon; the wedge of land reclaimed between them took its name plainly from being in the middle: Nakajima, the 'middle island.'

In 1589 the warlord Mori Terumoto chose this delta, then known as Goka, as the site for a new castle. The castle's own history describes him surveying the site from the hills around the delta before building began that year, and says the name Hiroshima may date from this moment. Terumoto moved into the unfinished castle in 1591; the stone walls were finished in 1593 and the castle in 1599. A commercial guidebook of 1925 sums up what followed: after Terumoto lost the domain at Sekigahara in 1600, the Fukushima and then the Asano lords governed the delta for more than 270 years, and the small trades that grew up under their rule were, the guide notes, still shaping the city's industry in the twentieth century. A companion atlas the city published in 1925 reproduces seven comparative maps of the castle town, from Terumoto's own era to 1877.

By 1900 a guidebook to the city could describe Nakajima precisely: bounded by the Motoyasu River to the east and the Hon River to the west, its northern tip at a bend called Jisenji-no-hana and its southern edge running down to the reclaimed fields of Yoshijima, the district was, in the guide's words, 'just like an islet of its own.' A bridge already crossed the river at the fork, and the same book, which writes its name 相合 ('joined together'), explains it: two spans, east and west, met as one. Nearby stood Motoyasu Bridge, a 28-ken timber span with iron railings on the old national highway, which the guide calls, together with Honkawa Bridge, the busiest crossing in the city.

In neighboring Kako-machi stood the district's civic quarter: the prefectural office and prefectural assembly hall, both built in 1878, a prefectural hospital, and, sited by 1900 in Nakajima Shinmachi itself, the city hall and city assembly. Behind the hospital lay Yorakuen, a former Asano-family villa turned public garden with an artificial hill, a pond and a boulder locals said had cost a fortune to move; it opened to visitors only on Sundays and festival days. Two temples anchored the district's religious life: Tenmangu in Tenjin-cho, a shrine to Sugawara no Michizane that Mori Terumoto had transferred from the family's old castle at Koriyama, and Seiganji in Zaimoku-cho, a major Jodo-sect temple whose founder is said to have raised its halls on what was then open reed-flat.

sections.heading: A commercial quarter comes of age

paragraphs.text: War and trade brought Hiroshima's economy a series of jolts. A 1925 commercial guide traces the sequence: the Meiji Restoration opened a 'national economy' era; the wars with China and Russia turned the city into the leading commercial center west of Osaka; and the First World War, together with Ujina harbor, whose construction the prefecture completed in 1889, drew large modern enterprises and made Hiroshima, in the guide's phrase, a hinge between the industrial belt of northern Kyushu and the Hanshin region around Osaka and Kobe. Nakajima Honmachi had been the city's leading shopping street since the last years of the Edo period. Its heyday passed in the 1910s and 1920s, but its shops kept trading, and in March 1929 the kimono merchant Taishoya opened a modern three-story reinforced-concrete store, with a basement, on its main street.

Just before the bombing, by the estimate of the city's 1971 war-damage record as reported by the local newspaper, some 1,330 households and 4,370 people lived in the district's seven neighborhood associations: Nakajima Honmachi, the two Tenjin-cho associations, Zaimoku-cho, Kobiki-cho, Moto-yanagi-cho and Nakajima Shinmachi. Family photographs published by the same paper show what was there: a footwear shop on the Tenjin-cho street along the Motoyasu River, a dye shop whose owner and three of his family were killed by the bomb, a trading company on Zaimoku-cho, and on Moto-yanagi-cho a confectioner's branch office in a building that had been a bank's head office until 1927. Upstream, the Aioi Bridge had been rebuilt in 1932 and, in 1934, extended into a distinctive T-shape.

The T-shaped Aioi Bridge, unmistakable from the air, is said to have been the aiming point for the atomic bomb dropped on the morning of 6 August 1945. The bomb missed by about 300 meters and exploded above Shima Hospital, where a clinic of the same name stands today. The blast and heat that followed obliterated Nakajima and the blocks around it, which lay between about 100 and 700 meters from the hypocenter; the city's own account of the district states simply that it suffered total destruction. That morning many students, and people mobilized from neighborhoods and workplaces, were at work clearing buildings for firebreaks around what is now Peace Boulevard; the city's account records that the students who gathered on the riverbanks, burned beyond recognition and begging for water, all died.

Individual buildings tell the same story at closer range. At the Taishoya building, which in wartime had become the 'Fuel Hall' of the prefectural fuel-rationing union, 37 staff were at work when the bomb fell some 170 meters away; every one of them died except Nomura Eizo, who happened to be in the basement fetching papers and became the building's only survivor. At Honkawa Elementary School, 410 meters from the hypocenter, the reinforced-concrete school building burned out completely, leaving only its shell, and then served as a relief station for the injured. The Industrial Promotion Hall, about 160 meters from the hypocenter, burned out too, but because the blast came down on it almost vertically the central part of the building did not collapse.

How many died is still not precisely known. The city's own current estimate, reached by combining several postwar surveys, is that approximately 140,000 people, plus or minus 10,000, had died by the end of December 1945 from the bombing's immediate and short-term effects; the city states plainly that this remains an estimate rather than a count of named individuals. Among the dead were Koreans then living or working in Hiroshima under Japan's colonial rule; the Peace Memorial Museum's guide to their memorial says that tens of thousands of Koreans were in the city and exposed to the bomb.

sections.heading: From ashes to a memorial city

paragraphs.text: Planning for what would replace Nakajima began astonishingly fast. Hiroshima Prefecture proposed setting aside the hypocenter area as a memorial zone as early as September 1945, a month after the bombing; the city's reconstruction council turned this into a concrete park plan by February 1946; and in November 1946 a park on the Nakajima district was written into the national reconstruction plan for Hiroshima. The legal foundation followed in May 1949, when the Diet passed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law, a special statute that applied to Hiroshima alone; reconstruction, held back until then by a severe shortage of money, only gathered pace after it. A design competition that summer drew 145 entries; the winning scheme, submitted by a group led by the architect Kenzo Tange, set the park's Cenotaph, the ruined Dome and the Peace Memorial Museum on a single sightline running north from the museum's raised colonnade.

Construction followed through the 1950s. Tange's saddle-roofed Cenotaph, its curved form recalling the clay houses once placed on ancient burial mounds, was unveiled on 6 August 1952 and carries an inscription whose English rendering reads 'Let all the souls here rest in peace, for we shall not repeat the evil.' The Peace Memorial Hall was completed in May 1955 and the Peace Memorial Museum in August. The transformation of the old commercial district into parkland was not, however, immediate: barracks put up by people living on the planned park site remained until about 1959, fourteen years after the bombing.

Peace Boulevard, the 100-meter-wide road along the park's southern edge, followed the same slow path. Japan's reconstruction policy of December 1945 had planned 24 roads at least 100 meters wide in seven cities; only three were built, two in Nagoya and this one. In 1955 a candidate who promised to halve its width and build municipal housing on the rest was elected mayor. Persuaded to drop the pledge, he launched a tree-donation campaign instead, and in 1957 and 1958 more than 100,000 trees and saplings arrived from across Japan and abroad to plant the road.

Preserving the Dome's skeleton was, for two decades, an open question; some Hiroshima residents wanted the dangerous, painful ruin demolished rather than kept as a landmark. In July 1966 the city council resolved to preserve it, and a fundraising drive raised 66,197,816 yen from donors in Japan and abroad for the first preservation work in 1967. In the early 1990s a nationwide petition asking for World Heritage status, finally signed by 1,653,996 people, was adopted by both houses of the Diet in 1994; the government designated the Dome a national historic site in June 1995 and nominated it that September, and in December 1996 UNESCO inscribed it on the World Heritage List; the city's own framing describes it as a monument meant to convey the bombing's devastation to the whole world.

Other memorials arrived later still, and not without dispute. A memorial to Korean victims of the bomb was erected in April 1970, but outside the park proper, near the west end of Honkawa Bridge, The Peace Memorial Museum's guide explains the site: Prince Yi U, of Korea's royal family, was found near there after the bombing. Calls to move the memorial into the park grew over the following decades, and after talks between the city and those concerned it was moved inside the park in July 1999. The Hiroshima National Peace Memorial Hall for the Atomic Bomb Victims, designed by Tange's firm and built mostly underground, opened on 1 August 2002.

Little of Nakajima's street grid survives in the park's lawns, but several fixed points let a visitor locate it. The Dome still stands where the Industrial Promotion Hall did. The Aioi Bridge, rebuilt in 1983 on the same T-shaped plan, still forks toward the park's northern tip close to where the 1900 guidebook placed its wooden predecessor; a newel post from the wartime bridge, still marked by the blast, is kept at the bridge end, and a bent piece of its girder is in the Peace Memorial Museum. The Rest House, once the Taishoya kimono shop and restored in 2020 close to its original look, keeps the basement where Nomura Eizo survived; it is open to visitors.

Across the Hon River to the west, part of the gutted Honkawa school building is kept as the school's peace museum. The Cenotaph's sightline to the Dome was drawn by Tange's plan, not inherited from the old town; the old street pattern is easier to find at the Rest House, beside Motoyasu Bridge, the crossing that carried the old highway into Nakajima. On the evening of 6 August, paper lanterns are still floated on the Motoyasu River, a practice the city traces to families of the dead in the years soon after the war.

timeline.what: Mori Terumoto begins building Hiroshima Castle on the Ota River delta, at a site then called Goka.
After Terumoto's defeat at Sekigahara, the Fukushima and then Asano lords govern the delta for more than 270 years of castle-town growth.
The prefectural office and prefectural assembly hall are built in Kako-machi, next to Nakajima.
Construction of Ujina harbor is completed, opening the delta to ocean shipping.
A city guidebook describes Nakajima, between the Motoyasu and Hon rivers, as 'just like an islet of its own.'
The Hiroshima Prefectural Commercial Exhibition Hall, designed by the Czech architect Jan Letzel, is completed; renamed the Industrial Promotion Hall in 1933, it is today's Atomic Bomb Dome.
The kimono merchant Taishoya opens a three-story reinforced-concrete store on Nakajima Honmachi's main street; later the Rest House.
Aioi Bridge is rebuilt, then extended in 1934 into its distinctive T-shape.
The atomic bomb, said to have been aimed at Aioi Bridge, explodes about 300 meters away above Shima Hospital; Nakajima and the surrounding district are destroyed.

A park on the Nakajima district enters the national reconstruction plan (November 1946); the Diet passes the Hiroshima Peace Memorial City Construction Law (May 1949) and a design competition is won by a group led by Kenzo Tange.
Tange's Cenotaph is unveiled (6 August 1952); the Peace Memorial Hall and the Peace Memorial Museum are completed (May and August 1955).
The last barracks on the park site disappear, about fourteen years after the bombing.

The Korean Atomic Bomb Victims Memorial is erected outside the park (1970); the Dome is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1996); the Korean memorial is moved inside the park (1999); the National Peace Memorial Hall opens (2002).

caveats: Casualty totals for the bombing remain officially uncertain; this dossier uses the city's own current estimate (about 140,000 plus or minus 10,000 dead by the end of December 1945), which the city itself describes as an estimate rather than a count of named individuals.

Several early-twentieth-century civic buildings described here (the prefectural office, city hall, hospital, Yorakuen) stood in the adjoining blocks of Kako-machi and Nakajima Shinmachi rather than on the Nakajima Honmachi islet itself; this dossier follows each source's own place names rather than imposing modern district boundaries retroactively.
The 1900 guidebook's OCR text is corrupted in places; a passage purporting to explain a personal-name origin for Motoyasu Bridge was too garbled to use with confidence and has been omitted.

The 1900 guidebook writes the bridge at the fork as 相合橋; today's Aioi Bridge is written 相生橋. The guidebook places it at the same fork, but no source consulted states outright that the two names belong to the same crossing.
